A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ICA data-selection framework. All pages, including appendices, are readable, and retained equations, algorithms, tables and examples can be matched across revisions. Internal reporting inconsistencies do not prevent comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original SFT, DPO and SimPO experiments across LLaMA and Qwen models, together with ablations, runtime measurements and LoRA results.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds GSM8K results, additional baseline comparisons, training-seed variability and holdout-use controls.

M1.justification: The ICA loss difference, min-max weights, weighted gradients, nearest-neighbor demonstrations and periodic scoring remain unchanged in Equations 6–9 and Algorithms 1–2. v1 already permits hard selection and evaluates percentile filtering; v2's matched subset-selection comparisons use that existing scoring framework.

E1.justification: v2 retains Alpaca, Yahoo_Answers_Topics, UltraFeedback and SHP-2, and adds GSM8K mathematical reasoning. Experiments use both original training data and data with intentionally corrupted chain-of-thought annotations, substantially extending coverage beyond the original instruction and preference-alignment tasks.

E2.justification: LESS and GREATS, previously cited but not evaluated, become actual SFT comparators on Yahoo_Answers_Topics and GSM8K in Tables 14–16. The original comparisons against standard training, RHO-Loss and One-shot remain.

E3.justification: New protocols introduce PPL/BERTScore, zero-shot CoT Pass@1, matched top-5% and per-batch 50% selection, and holdout-exclusion and holdout-only controls. Appendix B.1 also changes Yahoo training counts from 1,000 examples per other domain and 12,000 total to 10,000 and a stated 100,300 total. This is a reported setting revision, without evidence that retained experiments were rerun; the new total does not reconcile with the stated sampling recipe.

E4.justification: v2 adds corrupted-CoT robustness experiments, controls testing whether gains depend on training on holdout examples or on the broader training set, and an analysis of ICA-weight dynamics across updates (Section 5.5 and Appendices C.4–C.6). The original k, update-frequency, filtering and embedding ablations remain.

E5.justification: v1 reports repeated GPT-evaluation variability for one trained model. v2 specifies that these were three evaluations and adds means and standard deviations across three independent training seeds for both LLaMA-8B and Qwen-8B on Yahoo (Appendix B.2, Table 5). This extends uncertainty assessment to training randomness; the main experiments remain single runs.

E6.justification: Tables 1–3 retain every numerical result, while v2 adds seed aggregates, absolute metrics, baseline comparisons, runtime measurements and holdout-control outcomes. For example, new Table 15 reports corrupted-GSM8K accuracy of 79.95%/83.04% for ICA reweighting versus 52.75%/62.40% for unweighted SFT on LLaMA/Qwen-8B. These are newly reported experiments, not performance improvements between versions under unchanged settings.

T1.justification: Equation 3 changes from an approximate relation to an asserted equality, and the accompanying optimal-selection statement loses its approximation qualifier. Appendix A explicitly formulates the existing conditional-independence assumption but otherwise retains the derivation. No new theorem or ICA approximation-error proof is supplied.

C1.justification: v2 removes the abstract's claim that ICA is equivalent to a first-order update toward the holdout optimum under local linearization. The introduction instead describes approximating the effects of parameter updates. The central claims of efficient, reference-free scoring and improved SFT/DPO/SimPO alignment remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations connecting excessive demonstrations to lower relevance and diminishing benefits of score updates to stabilizing weights. It interprets the new noise and holdout controls and changes the limitation from ICA being inherently off-policy to the experiments using off-policy paradigms. The existing concern about unrepresentative holdouts remains.

D1.justification: v2 documents the GSM8K holdout size, corruption fraction and example corruption operations, and describes reimplementing LESS/GREATS from their public code with specified selection fractions. The original hyperparameter table, hardware and prompts are retained. The exact corruption recipe and weaker model are unspecified, and both versions still promise a future code release.

R1.justification: v2 adds references for GSM8K, an in-context-learning survey and BERTScore. Section 5.2 also contrasts ICA's Bayesian scoring with the first-order approximations and computational requirements of LESS/GREATS. The related-work section and positioning relative to RHO-Loss otherwise remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: There are targeted rewrites of the abstract, methodological explanation and experimental discussion, plus an added author. Experimental-setup paragraphs are reordered, and existing LoRA results, prompts and examples are regrouped into Appendices C and D. The main narrative and section sequence remain recognizable.

P2.justification: v2 adds substantial tabular displays for training variability, absolute metrics, additional baselines, GSM8K and holdout controls. It reformats evaluation uncertainty as mean ± standard deviation, revises captions and headers, and rearranges appendix tables. The top-k labels change from 1/3/5 to 1/5/10, matching the existing prose. Figure 1 and the qualitative examples are retained and relocated.

improvement.justification: The new non-GPT metrics, GSM8K accuracy, independent training seeds and holdout controls address important weaknesses in v1's reliance on single trained models and judge-based target matching. LESS/GREATS comparisons also strengthen the evidence against relevant alternatives. The inconsistent Yahoo sample-count revision and stronger equality assertion in Equation 3 remain concerns, but the added controls and independent measurements provide a substantial net improvement in empirical support.
